feedback.pattern: Regression in remove() return value and tree structure after refactoring
feedback.explanation: This test passed in run 50 after remove() was refactored to use a return-value pattern (root = removeHelper(root, i, b)), but failed in run 53. The code diff at run 53 shows a change to the successor-finding logic for two-child node removal: the code switched from finding the in-order predecessor (bottom = cur.left, then traversing right) to finding the in-order successor (bottom = cur.right, then traversing left), with adjusted node replacement logic. This change caused test failures through run 54, which triggered a StackOverflowError indicating infinite recursion in the remove() method. Run 55 introduced a rewrite of the successor-finding and node-replacement logic, adding a prev pointer to track the parent of the successor candidate and a comparison check (comp2) to bound the successor search. The test passed from run 55 onward.
nextSteps: Review the in-order successor algorithm: when removing a node with two children, the successor is the smallest node in the right subtree (found by going right once, then left as far as possible). Ensure the parent pointer is tracked so the successor can be unlinked from its original position before being spliced into the removed node's position.

Verify that removeHelper() correctly returns the modified subtree root at every recursive call site, especially after node replacement. The pattern root = removeHelper(root, i, b) ensures the tree structure is maintained even when the root itself is removed.
Test the two-child case in isolation: insert a small tree (e.g., 5, 3, 7, 2, 4, 6, 8), remove the root (5), and verify the tree structure is correct and the size is decremented properly.

diffs.note: Run 50: Simplified remove() to use return-value pattern (root = removeHelper) instead of void call, enabling proper tree reconnection.

diffs.note: Run 53: Changed successor-finding direction from left-subtree predecessor to right-subtree successor, but introduced incorrect node-replacement logic that caused tree corruption.

feedback.pattern: Sustained iterator logic errors across multiple traversal strategies
feedback.explanation: The in-order iterator failed across runs 26–40. Run 26 produced a null pointer exception during initialization. Run 27 patched this, but next() then returned incorrect values (expected 2 but got 1). Runs 28–30 showed no change in test outcome. Run 40 introduced a significant rewrite of the iterator's internal state machine. The code diff shows the addition of explicit flag management (pushing flag value 2 instead of 1) and a conditional check to avoid re-adding the current node's frame when it has already been processed and is about to be returned. The test passed from run 40 onward.
nextSteps: Understand the three-phase iterative in-order traversal: (1) push the node and go left, (2) pop and return the node, (3) push the right subtree. Use a flag or state variable to track which phase each stack frame is in, ensuring each node is visited exactly once in the correct order.

When implementing next(), carefully manage the stack so that after returning a node, the iterator is positioned to process the right subtree on the next call. Avoid re-pushing nodes that have already been returned.
Test the iterator on a simple tree (e.g., 2, 1, 3) and manually trace the stack state after each next() call to verify the traversal order matches in-order (1, 2, 3).

feedback.pattern: Two-child node removal logic error causing incorrect tree size
feedback.explanation: This test failed across runs 45–55 with a size mismatch error (expected 3 but got 15 or similar), indicating that remove() was not properly decrementing the tree size or was leaving nodes in the tree. The test passed in run 50 initially, but failed in run 53 when the successor-finding logic was changed from predecessor to successor without corresponding updates to the node-replacement code. Run 54 produced a StackOverflowError in the remove() method, indicating infinite recursion in the helper function. Run 55 rewrote the successor-finding algorithm with a prev pointer to track the parent of the successor candidate and a comparison-based loop termination (comp2 comparison check in the code diff). The test passed from run 55 onward.
nextSteps: Ensure that removeHelper() decrements the tree size (or returns a flag indicating removal) exactly once per successful removal, regardless of which case (leaf, one child, two children) is executed. The size should be decremented before returning from the helper function.

For the two-child case, implement the successor-finding loop with a clear termination condition: traverse right once, then left until reaching a node with no left child. Track the parent of the successor so it can be unlinked and reconnected correctly.
Add a size assertion after each remove() call in a test: verify that size() decreases by exactly 1 if the element was found, and remains unchanged if the element was not in the tree.

diffs.note: Run 55: Rewrote the two-child removal logic with explicit parent tracking (prev pointer) and a comparison-based loop (comp2) to correctly identify and unlink the in-order successor, fixing the size mismatch and infinite recursion.

feedback.pattern: Incorrect linear search logic in containsNonBST() method
feedback.explanation: This test failed across runs 1–9. Runs 1–2 produced a compilation error due to missing method implementation. Run 3 added an implementation of containsNonBST(), but the method returned false when it should have returned true, indicating a logic error in the linear search. Runs 4–8 showed no change in test outcome. Run 9 introduced a complete implementation of containsNonBST() that performs a full tree traversal to search for the target value without relying on BST ordering. The code diff shows the addition of the isEmpty() helper method and the full containsNonBST() method body. The test passed from run 9 onward.
nextSteps: Implement containsNonBST() as a full tree search that does not assume BST ordering: recursively check if the target value matches the current node, or if it exists in the left subtree, or if it exists in the right subtree. Use short-circuit evaluation (return true as soon as a match is found) to avoid unnecessary traversals.

Distinguish between contains() (which uses BST ordering to prune the search space) and containsNonBST() (which must visit all nodes). The latter is useful for verifying tree integrity or searching in a corrupted tree.

Test containsNonBST() on a tree where the target value is in the right subtree of the root but would be pruned by BST logic (e.g., searching for 10 in a tree with root 5, left child 3, right child 7, right-right child 10). Verify it returns true.

feedback.pattern: Pre-order iterator state machine logic errors across multiple runs
feedback.explanation: The pre-order iterator failed across runs 19–25. Run 19 produced incorrect hasNext() logic. Run 21 inverted the boolean return, but run 22 then showed the iterator returning null instead of values. Run 23 adjusted the next() logic but returned the wrong value (7 instead of 5). Run 25 introduced a substantial rewrite of the iterator initialization and state management. The code diff shows the addition of version tracking (to detect concurrent modifications), explicit initialization of the stack with the root node (guarded by a null check), and version capture at construction time. The test passed from run 25 onward.
nextSteps: Implement pre-order traversal as a stack-based iterative walk: initialize the stack with the root node, and in next(), pop the current node, return it, then push its right child (if not null) and left child (if not null) in that order. This ensures children are processed in the correct pre-order sequence.

Use a version field to detect concurrent modifications: capture the tree's version at iterator construction, and throw ConcurrentModificationException if the tree is modified during iteration. This helps catch bugs where the tree structure changes while iterating.
Test the pre-order iterator on a simple tree (e.g., 5, 3, 7, 2, 4, 6, 8) and verify the traversal order is correct (5, 3, 2, 4, 7, 6, 8). Manually trace the stack state after each next() call.

diffs.note: Run 25: Rewrote iterator initialization to properly guard the root push with a null check, added version tracking for concurrent modification detection, and refactored the state machine logic to correctly implement pre-order traversal.
